X.statement: The set of all finite linear combinations of elements of S satisfies the closure axioms and is therefore a subspace of V; it is called the subspace spanned by S, or the linear span of S. If S is empty the span is defined to be the set consisting of the zero element alone.

Y.statement: The column space of A consists of all linear combinations of the columns of A, i.e. all vectors Ax; it is a subspace of R^m.

X.statement: A real linear space V is said to have an inner product if to each pair of elements x, y there corresponds a unique real number (x, y) satisfying four axioms: symmetry, distributivity (linearity), homogeneity in the scalar, and positivity for nonzero x. Apostol defines the product axiomatically rather than by a specific formula.

Y.statement: Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero. The test is v^T w = 0.

X.statement: Given a linear space V, a nonempty subset S of V is called a subspace of V if S is itself a linear space under the same operations of addition and multiplication by scalars.

Y.statement: A subspace of a vector space is a set of vectors (including 0) closed under addition and scalar multiplication, so all linear combinations stay in the set.

X.statement: If a linear space V has a basis of n elements, the integer n is called the dimension of V. The space consisting of the zero element alone is said to have dimension 0.

Y.statement: The dimension of a space is the number of vectors in every basis for that space. It counts the degrees of freedom in the space; the dimension of R^n is n. We never speak of the rank of a space or the dimension of a basis.

X.statement: A real linear space V is said to have an inner product if to each pair of elements x, y there corresponds a unique real number (x, y) satisfying four axioms: symmetry, distributivity (linearity), homogeneity in the scalar, and positivity for nonzero x. Apostol defines the product axiomatically rather than by a specific formula.

Y.statement: The dot product of v and w is written v . w = v^T w, so the orthogonality condition is v^T w = 0.

X.statement: The dot product x . y of two vectors in V_n, defined in Chapter 12 by the sum of the products of corresponding components. It is the concrete product in terms of which lengths and angles in V_n were defined, and it is the model that the inner product generalizes; in V_n one may take (x, y) = x . y.

Y.statement: The dot product of v and w is written v . w = v^T w, so the orthogonality condition is v^T w = 0.

X.statement: In a Euclidean space V, two elements x and y are called orthogonal if their inner product is zero. The zero element is orthogonal to every element of V, and it is the only element orthogonal to itself.

Y.statement: Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero. The test is v^T w = 0.
